digest.top_line: RTOG 9601: 24mo bicalutamide 150mg added to 64.8Gy salvage RT in pN0 post-RP PSA recurrence → 12-yr OS 76.3% vs 71.3%, HR 0.77 (0.59-0.99).
digest.tldr: Prostate leads: at 13-yr f/u, RTOG 9601's bicalutamide OS benefit tracks entry PSA (HR 1.13 at <0.7 vs 0.45 at >1.5 ng/ml, post hoc). SBRT motion data flag the inferior margin (BIR-derived 7.0 mm). In seminoma, Classen IIA/B RT (6-yr RFS 95.3%/88.9%, 100% in-field control) and Paly's nodal map inform para-aortic field design.

sites.intro: Two seminoma RT field papers: a prospective outcomes series for the dog-leg field and a nodal map arguing for smaller vascular-based CTVs.

studies.name: Nodal metastasis mapping in seminoma (Paly et al.)
studies.tldr: 84% of 145 imaging-positive nodes were para-aortic; 99% fell within a 2.5cm lateral/posterior, 2.1cm anterior arterial expansion, supporting smaller vascular-based CTVs.
details: 🔍 CS IIA/B or recurrent CS I seminoma after orchiectomy; nodes ≤5 cm, no distant mets

details.text: 🔍 145 radiographically positive nodes; >1 cm short axis on CT (86 pts) or nanoparticle MRI uptake (4 pts)

details: ⚠️ Nodes not typically biopsy-proven; positivity by imaging alone, single-radiologist review
📊 Pelvic-only relapse: 4 pts (4%)

subdetails: Left-sided: no PA nodes right of the aorta, none renal hilar or above L1
Right-sided: 8 contralateral PA nodes (13%) in 5 (12%) pts
Right-sided: none above L2; one right renal hilar node

details.text: 📊 Proposed CTV: 2.5 cm lateral/posterior (excluding vertebral bodies), 2.1 cm anterior from arterial vasculature → covers 99% of nodes

details: 📊 Superior border: 1 cm above right renal artery or 1.5 cm above left renal artery, whichever lies more inferiorly

details.text: 📊 5 (3.5%) nodes in 4 pts fell outside a Classen field: 3 left inguinal, 1 gonadal-vein, 1 right renal hilar

details: 🔗 vs Classen extended field (NCCN / EGCCCG-endorsed): inferior border at acetabular rim supported; covers pelvic but not inguinal nodes
⚠️ Pattern-of-relapse map, not an outcomes study: no in-field control or SMN data for the reduced field
⚠️ Many pts had only one CT, so original node position before reaching size threshold is estimated

verdict.rationale: Retrospective imaging-defined node map with no prospective validation of the reduced CTV; authors restrict use to a research setting. Recurrence and toxicity under the smaller field remain untested.
verdict.audience: CS IIA/B or recurrent CS I seminoma post-orchiectomy, nodes ≤5 cm

studies.significance: The superior border is where the volume saving lives: no nodes sat above L1 for left-sided or above L2 for right-sided primaries, so a border 1 to 1.5 cm above the renal arteries replaces the T10/T11 edge. Laterality also matters: left-sided primaries produced no PA nodes right of the aorta, which questions routine right-of-IVC coverage.
studies.monday_clinic: For a CS IIA/B seminoma being planned for RT, this map backs contouring the nodal CTV off the arterial vasculature with a lowered superior border, inside a protocol; it does not extend to pts with prior scrotal or inguinal surgery, where the inferior border needs extending to 1 cm below the femoral head.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: **Retrospective multi-institutional mapping study**, 4 academic centers, pts diagnosed 1996-2011. Each imaging-positive node was transferred to a CT template by its relationship to the aorta and renal arteries, with craniocaudal scaling for pt height.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: **N=90, CS IIA/B or recurrent CS I seminoma after orchiectomy**, nodes ≤5 cm, no distant metastases. 40 pts (44%) relapsed on surveillance at a median 8.5 mo (range 3.2-50.4); 48 left-sided, 41 right-sided, 1 bilateral.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: Proposed initial CTV: **2.5 cm lateral and posterior** (excluding vertebral bodies) and **2.1 cm anterior** from the arterial vasculature, superior border **1 cm above the right or 1.5 cm above the left renal artery**. Inferior border at the acetabular rim per Classen; extend to 1 cm below the femoral head after prior pelvic surgery; for adjuvant RT in CS I, caudal border 1 cm below the aortic bifurcation.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: 145 nodes, average 1.6 per pt, median size 1.8 cm. **99% of nodes** fell within the proposed expansion; 2 atypical right-sided nodes (1.4%) were excluded, and **96.6% of nodal metastases** fell within an area smaller than conventional fields.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: The **Classen extended field**, backed by a 2003 phase II trial and endorsed by NCCN and the European consensus group, would have missed 5 (3.5%) nodes. The authors cite **MRC TE10**, where smaller fields reduced short-term GI distress and leukopenia, and an earlier vascular-based scheme (Martin et al.) that kept a T10/T11 superior border with a 1.4 cm aorta/IVC expansion.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents CS IIA/B or surveillance-relapsed CS I seminoma with nodes ≤5 cm after orchiectomy. Does not represent CS IIC/III disease, which was excluded and is typically managed with chemotherapy.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Nodes were **imaging-defined, not biopsy-proven**. Many pts had a single CT, so a node's position before it reached size criteria is estimated. Failures that would fall outside the reduced field cannot be captured by a relapse map.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The data support a CTV built on vascular rather than bony anatomy and looking more like an RPLND template. The SMN reduction is **modelled, not measured**: no pt here was treated with the proposed field.

studies.interpretation:
The argument here is anatomic, not clinical. The paper takes the place seminoma actually relapses in, the retroperitoneum near the great vessels, and asks whether the bony-landmark fields of the pre-CT era cover far more tissue than the disease needs. The map says they do. The volume saving sits mainly at the superior border: no imaging-positive node sat above L1 for left-sided primaries or above L2 for right-sided ones, yet the conventional para-aortic and Classen fields reach up to the T10/T11 interspace. Moving that edge to just above the renal arteries matches the cranial boundary of an RPLND template, so the radiation target comes to look like the surgical one. Two small series the authors cite, which used T12/L1 or T11/T12 superior borders, saw no relapses above the field; that is reassuring but thin.

The laterality finding may matter more for planning than the craniocaudal one. Left-sided primaries produced no para-aortic nodes to the right of the aorta, while right-sided primaries crossed over in 5 (12%) pts. This fits the long-standing RPLND mapping literature (Donohue's non-seminoma series) and the known lymphatic drainage asymmetry. It implies that a symmetric field around both the aorta and the IVC overtreats the left-sided pt. Because the authors mapped nodes only against arterial structures and left out the IVC as too variable, a reader who adopts this CTV is accepting a deliberate simplification. The two excluded right-sided nodes (renal hilum, gonadal vein) show where that simplification can fail.

How much confidence the 99% coverage figure deserves depends on three method choices, all of which push toward optimism. First, positivity was set by size on imaging, not by pathology, so a reactive node above 1 cm counts and a sub-centimetre deposit does not. Second, each node was placed by its relation to the vessels at a single timepoint, and in many pts there was only one scan, so the site where a node first seeded is inferred from where it was once it had grown. Third, and most important, a relapse map cannot show where a pt would fail after treatment with the smaller field. The recurrences seen came after surveillance or at presentation, not after reduced-field RT, and microscopic disease left outside a tighter CTV would only show up in a prospective series. The authors say this themselves when they restrict the field to research use.

The benefit side is just as unmeasured. The case for shrinking the field rests on second malignancy risk that rises with dose and volume, on the TE10 experience of less acute GI toxicity and leukopenia with smaller fields, and on modelling. No SMN reduction was observed here and none could have been. The authors also argue that because salvage works so well, a small excess of out-of-field relapse may be an acceptable price for fewer fatal second cancers. That trade-off is reasonable but it is an assumption, not a result.

What would make this wrong? A prospective cohort treated with the vascular CTV showing marginal or superior-border failures above what the excluded 1.4% suggests. Without that, the study is best read as a contouring hypothesis with a clear anatomic basis. It is most useful for the left-sided CS IIA/B pt, where the contralateral and superior reductions are best supported by the map.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: The superior border is where the volume saving lives: no nodes sat above L1 for left-sided or L2 for right-sided primaries, so a border 1 to 1.5 cm above the renal arteries replaces T10/T11. Left-sided primaries had no PA nodes right of the aorta, which questions routine right-of-IVC coverage.

open_questions: Marginal and out-of-field failure rate with vascular-based reduced CTV
Measured second malignancy reduction with smaller seminoma fields
Role of nanoparticle-enhanced MRI in defining sub-centimetre nodes

studies.name: Classen stage IIA/B seminoma RT trial
studies.tldr: 6-yr RFS 95.3% (IIA, 30 Gy) and 88.9% (IIB, 36 Gy) with para-aortic/ipsilateral high iliac RT; 100% in-field control, DSS 100%.
details: 🔍 Prospective multicenter observational study, 30 German centers, enrolled 1991-1994
🔍 N=94 enrolled; 87 assessable (66 IIA, 21 IIB); 7 lost to follow-up and excluded
🔍 Median f/u 70 mo (range 3-111)
🔍 Pure seminoma, Royal Marsden IIA (<2 cm) or IIB (2-5 cm); AFP-elevated pts excluded

subdetails: AP-PA hockey-stick: para-aortic/paracaval + ipsilateral high iliac nodes
Upper border cranial rim T11; lower border cranial rim ipsilateral acetabulum
Enlarged nodes covered with 2-cm safety margin; no boost
2.0 Gy/fx: 30 Gy for IIA, 36 Gy for IIB; 4-20 MV photons

details: 📊 Primary endpoint: RFS at 5 yr; reported as actuarial 6-yr RFS

details.text: 📊 Patterns of failure (4 relapses, all per-protocol pts)
subdetails: IIA: 1 mediastinal, 1 left-sided field-edge, at 33 and 40 mo
IIB: 1 mediastinal, 1 mediastinal/pulmonary, at 10 and 17 mo
No pelvic or inguinal recurrence; 100% in-field control
All salvaged with platinum-based chemo; all in continuous CR

details: 📊 Acute G3: nausea 8% IIA, nausea and diarrhea 10% IIB; no G4
📊 No late toxicity beyond 1 case of G1 skin hyperpigmentation; no second malignancy to date
⚠️ Single-arm, no randomised comparator vs chemo; IIB arm only 21 pts, wide CI
⚠️ Major protocol violations in 22 pts (25.3%), including dose deviations and bilateral iliac fields
⚠️ 70-mo median f/u too short for late cardiac or second-cancer risk
🔗 Sourced comparators: modified EP relapse 9% with 33% G3/4 leukopenia; carboplatin alone failure 15%

verdict.rationale: Single-arm observational design with no randomised chemo comparator; small IIB cohort and 70-mo median f/u insufficient for late-effect endpoints.
verdict.audience: Pure seminoma, Royal Marsden CS IIA/B, post-orchiectomy, AFP normal

studies.significance: The target-volume read is the transferable one: a hockey-stick field limited to para-aortic plus ipsilateral high iliac nodes produced no pelvic or inguinal failure and one field-edge relapse, with all other failures supradiaphragmatic. That argues against both bilateral pelvic and prophylactic mediastinal or supraclavicular coverage at 30 Gy (IIA) and 36 Gy (IIB).
studies.monday_clinic: In pure seminoma CS IIA (<2 cm) with normal AFP, this supports 30 Gy dog-leg RT as an option with salvageable failures; it gives thinner footing for IIB, where 21 pts carry a CI down to 74.4%, and none for bulkier IIC disease.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Prospective **multicenter observational** study, 30 centers in Germany, enrolled April 1991 to March 1994. **N=94** enrolled, **87 assessable**; median follow-up **70 mo** (range 3-111). Analyzed in the sense of intention-to-treat, unlike the earlier per-protocol report.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Histologically confirmed **pure testicular seminoma, Royal Marsden CS IIA (<2 cm) or IIB (2-5 cm)**, after high inguinal orchiectomy, staged by CT chest/abdomen/pelvis. **Elevated AFP excluded**; βHCG up to 200 IU/L admitted from year 2. 66 IIA, 21 IIB; median age 32.5 and 32 yr.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: AP-PA opposed fields to **para-aortic/paracaval + ipsilateral high iliac nodes** (hockey-stick), T11 to acetabular rim, gross nodes with a **2-cm margin**, no boost. **2.0 Gy/fx to 30 Gy (IIA) or 36 Gy (IIB)**; median doses 30 Gy (26-36) and 36 Gy (36-37).

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: **Primary:** relapse-free survival at 5 yr. **Secondary:** disease-specific survival (expected ≥95% at 5 yr), acute and late GI and cutaneous toxicity.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: **6-yr RFS 95.3%** (95% CI 88.9-100%) for IIA and **88.9%** (95% CI 74.4-100%) for IIB. Four relapses (2 mediastinal, 1 mediastinal/pulmonary, 1 field-edge), all salvaged with platinum chemo; **100% in-field control, DSS 100%**.

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: Acute toxicity dominated by G1 nausea (53% IIA, 52% IIB); **G3 nausea 8% IIA, G3 nausea and diarrhea 10% IIB, no G4**. No late GI toxicity or peptic ulceration; one G1 skin hyperpigmentation; no second malignancy reported to date.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Against the comparators the authors cite, modified EP carried a **9% relapse rate with 33% G3/4 leukopenia** and carboplatin alone a **15% failure rate**, while carboplatin followed by infradiaphragmatic RT gave **7.1% (IIA) and 5.3% (IIB)** relapse. Historic IIB series reported relapse **up to 33%** with larger fields.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents pure seminoma CS IIA/B with normal AFP after inguinal orchiectomy, treated with a dog-leg field. Does not represent CS IIC or bulkier nodal disease, AFP-elevated tumors, or pts considered for RPLND or chemo de-escalation.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: A quarter of pts had **major protocol violations**, including dose deviations and bilateral iliac fields, which blurs the field-size claim. IIA RFS of 95.3% is stated for the no/minor-violation group, with **100% in major violators**. Seven pts lost to follow-up were excluded from the final analysis.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: Failures clustered in the mediastinum and lungs, not the pelvis, so the reduced ipsilateral field held while the residual risk sits outside any infradiaphragmatic volume. The study was **not designed to test reduced portals** against larger fields, and it cannot settle late cardiac or second-cancer risk.

studies.interpretation:
The trial's lasting contribution is about target volume rather than about whether radiation works in stage II seminoma. Before it, stage II fields routinely covered the entire ipsilateral iliac and inguinal chain and often the contralateral pelvis. Here, all but five of the patients were treated to a limited hockey-stick volume covering only para-aortic and ipsilateral high iliac nodes, and there was no pelvic or inguinal recurrence. The single in-region failure was a lateral para-aortic field-edge relapse. The other three relapses were mediastinal or mediastinal/pulmonary, which no infradiaphragmatic field would have prevented and which the authors use to argue against prophylactic mediastinal or supraclavicular coverage. That pattern-of-failure logic is the part of this paper that still transfers to practice: the residual risk after dog-leg RT is distant and supradiaphragmatic, not marginal pelvic.

Confidence should be split by stage. The IIA cohort is reasonably sized at 66 patients and its 6-year RFS of 95.3% has a lower confidence bound of 88.9%. The IIB cohort is 21 patients, its 88.9% RFS carries a lower bound of 74.4%, and two of four relapses came from this small group within 17 months. A reader treating a 4-5 cm node should not read the IIB number as a precise estimate. The authors also concede the study was not built to show that reduced portals beat larger ones; it shows only that they did not visibly fail. And the field-size argument is weakened by the protocol deviations: 22 patients had major violations, five received bilateral iliac treatment, and the IIA RFS of 95.3% is reported for patients with minor or no violations, with 100% in major violators. That inversion is reassuring about robustness of outcome but makes the per-group numbers harder to interpret cleanly.

The comparative argument against chemotherapy rests on cited series rather than a randomised comparison. The authors set their result against a modified EP regimen with a 9% relapse rate and 33% grade 3/4 leukopenia, single-agent carboplatin with 15% failure, and carboplatin followed by infradiaphragmatic RT with relapse of 7.1% in IIA and 5.3% in IIB. These are cross-series comparisons across different eras and selection, so they support the claim that RT was not outperformed in its time, not that it was superior. The authors themselves expect full-dose EP or BEP to cure nearly all IIA/B patients, conceding that the trade is toxicity rather than control.

That trade is where the paper is least able to speak. With median follow-up of 70 months, the absence of second malignancies and cardiac events means little; the late harms that have since driven interest in RT de-escalation and in surgical approaches such as RPLND (tested in SEMS and PRIMETEST) emerge on a much longer horizon. All four relapses were salvaged with platinum chemotherapy, so disease-specific survival was 100%, which reframes the decision as one of total treatment burden over a young man's lifetime rather than cure rate.

For a radiation oncologist, the practical reads are: 30 Gy in 2 Gy fractions to a para-aortic plus ipsilateral high iliac field controlled IIA disease in-field in every patient, the authors noted three IIA patients treated to 26 Gy without in-field failure and suggest room for further dose reduction, and bilateral pelvic or mediastinal extension is not supported by this failure pattern. What would make it wrong is a longer follow-up showing late toxicity that outweighs the acute advantage over chemotherapy, which this dataset cannot exclude.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: A hockey-stick field limited to para-aortic plus ipsilateral high iliac nodes gave no pelvic or inguinal failure and 100% in-field control at 30 Gy (IIA) and 36 Gy (IIB). Failures were mediastinal, arguing against bilateral pelvic or supradiaphragmatic extension.
significance_by_specialty.medonc: All four relapses were mediastinal or pulmonary and all were salvaged with platinum chemo into continuous CR, so DSS was 100%. The chemo comparison relies on cited series (modified EP 9% relapse with 33% G3/4 leukopenia), not a randomised arm.

open_questions: Can dose drop below 30 Gy in stage IIA seminoma?
RT vs RPLND or reduced-intensity chemo for stage IIA/B
Late cardiac and second-cancer risk beyond 6 years

studies.name: Prostate SBRT intra-fraction motion and margins
studies.tldr: IFPM exceeded 6 mm/3 mm-posterior margins in 8/97 fractions, mostly posterior; BIR guidance gives 3.3-7.0 mm margins, larger only inferiorly.
details: 🔍 Retrospective analysis: 20 pts, 97 pre/post-treatment CBCT pairs
🔍 36.25 Gy in 5 fractions, no intra-fraction tracking, fiducial-based online match
🔍 Current clinical margins: 6 mm isotropic, 3 mm posterior
📊 Averaged 3D RMS IFPM 2.5 mm (2SD 4.2 mm)
📊 Motion mostly posterior (70%) and inferior (63%); RL evenly divided
📊 IFPM exceeded current margins in 8 of 97 fractions, 6 of them posterior

details.text: 📊 Margins by direction: current vs BIR updated guidance (mm)

details: 📐 Weak motion-time correlation: posterior ρ = 0.38, inferior ρ = 0.36
📐 Mean pre-to-post imaging interval 9 min, median 8 min 46 s

details.text: 🔍 Causes of excess motion (6 fractions evaluated)
subdetails: Bladder volume differences: n=3
Rectal volume differences: n=2
Pt movement: 1 fraction
No identified cause: 1 fraction

details: ⚠️ Delineation error is the largest margin component; excluding one outlier drops inferior margin 7 → 5.8 mm
⚠️ Delineation errors came from an MRI-only study, likely smaller than on CT or MR/CT fusion
⚠️ Match error assumed negligible, never measured
⚠️ Geometric surrogate only: no toxicity or biochemical control data

verdict.rationale: Single-institution retrospective geometric audit, 20 pts. No dosimetric or clinical outcome link, and delineation error was taken from a separate MRI-only study.
verdict.audience: Prostate cancer pts receiving SBRT 36.25 Gy/5fx, no intra-fraction tracking

studies.significance: The inferior margin is the only one the BIR guidance would widen (7.0 mm vs 6 mm), and that comes mostly from apex delineation error, not motion. Dropping one contouring outlier brings it to 5.8 mm. The real miss is posterior: 6 of 8 out-of-margin fractions breached the 3 mm rectal-side margin, so rectal and bladder consistency matter more than inferior expansion.
studies.monday_clinic: For a prostate SBRT pt on fiducial-matched CBCT without intra-fraction tracking, this supports the 6 mm isotropic, 3 mm posterior margin with attention to bladder and rectal reproducibility; it does not speak to tracked or MR-guided delivery.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: **Retrospective** single-centre audit: **97 pairs** of pre- and post-treatment CBCT from **20 pts**. Margins were derived from IFPM alone and from the **updated BIR geometric uncertainties guidance**.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: **36.25 Gy in 5 fractions**, delivered **without intra-fraction tracking**, online fiducial match on CBCT. Current PTV margins: **6 mm isotropic, 3 mm posterior**.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: Averaged 3D RMS IFPM **2.5 mm (4.2 mm)**, mostly **posterior (70%)** and **inferior (63%)**. IFPM exceeded current margins in **8 of 97 fractions**, six of them posterior. IFPM-only margins were **≤3.5 mm**. The BIR-derived margins covered motion in **92%** of fractions.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: The authors report intra-fraction margins close to other hypofractionated and SBRT series. A larger series (n=205) had **smaller systematic but similar random errors**, and prior work tied treatment times **<5 minutes** to less motion.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents prostate SBRT pts treated at 36.25 Gy/5fx with a fiducial CBCT match and no intra-fraction tracking. Does not represent tracked, gated, or MR-guided delivery, or CT/MR-fusion contouring workflows.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Deformation was set to 0. Match error was **assumed negligible, not measured**. AP and SI intra-fraction components were calculated per plane even though motion was directionally asymmetric. Two of the eight excess-motion fractions could not be assessed for cause.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: Current margins look **adequate except inferiorly** and could arguably be **reduced laterally**. The inferior expansion is driven by **apex delineation**, so contouring guidance may do more than adding margin. Any change should be weighed against **toxicity and biochemical outcomes** from the current trials.

studies.interpretation:
The useful finding here is less about how far the prostate moves during a five-fraction course and more about where the margin budget actually goes. Once the authors feed their measured errors into the updated BIR framework, intra-fraction motion and rotation turn out to be small contributors. Delineation dominates, and it dominates in the inferior direction, which is where the guidance asks for more margin than the department currently uses. So the case for a 7.0 mm inferior margin is mostly a case about apex contouring, not about motion. That changes what a department should do with the result: if one contouring outlier moves the inferior margin from 7 to 5.8 mm, the first lever is better delineation, not a larger PTV.

The posterior direction tells a different and more clinically pointed story. Six of the eight fractions where motion exceeded the current margin were posterior, where the margin is deliberately tight at 3 mm to protect the rectal wall. The BIR-derived posterior margin of 3.3 mm sits close to current practice, so the guidance does not argue for widening it. Yet that is where the geometric misses happen, and the identified causes (bladder and rectal volume changes, plus one episode of pt movement) are about preparation, not planning. For a radiation oncologist that points toward bowel and bladder protocols, faster image-to-beam time, or tracking, rather than margin expansion. The weak correlation between elapsed time and posterior or inferior drift, inside a narrow window of 6 to 15 minutes, means this series cannot say how much shorter delivery would help.

How much confidence should the numbers carry? Twenty pts and 97 fraction pairs is a modest sample for estimating population systematic error, and systematic error is exactly the component that dominates an SBRT margin recipe. Three of the inputs weaken the result in ways that do not obviously cancel. Delineation error came from an MRI-only study and is likely an underestimate for CT or fused MR/CT contouring, which would push margins up. Match error was assumed negligible, not measured, which also biases toward smaller margins. Deformation was set to zero. The real margin requirement is probably at least as large as reported, not smaller.

The authors' caution is the most defensible part of the paper. A geometric margin recipe is a surrogate. With steep SBRT dose gradients, incidental dose beyond the prostate may contribute to control, and current 6 mm/3 mm practice has not been shown to fail biochemically or to cause excess toxicity. Widening the inferior margin toward the apex and membranous urethra, or the posterior margin toward the rectum, has a toxicity cost this study does not measure. What would make the current margins wrong is clinical: a pattern of apical or posterior marginal failures in centres using these margins without tracking. Until outcome data show that, the result supports the status quo with better contouring and bladder and rectal preparation, and a lateral reduction is plausible but untested.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: The guidance would widen only the inferior margin (7.0 mm vs 6 mm), and that is driven by apex delineation, not motion; excluding one outlier gives 5.8 mm. Posterior is where 6 of 8 misses occurred, so bladder and rectal preparation matter more than PTV expansion.

open_questions: Does a wider inferior margin add toxicity without improving control?
Would intra-fraction tracking cut the posterior out-of-margin fractions?
Margin impact of delineation error on CT or MR/CT fusion

related_trials.brief_title: Stereotactic Radiotherapy of Prostate Cancer With Reduction of Safety Margins
related_trials.brief_summary: The study aims to reduce the PTV (Planning Target Volume) safety margins to 1-2 mm in stereotactic prostate radiotherapy for low- and medium-risk prostate cancers while maintaining a dose of 36.25 Gy in 5 fractions per day. By reducing the hems, the investigators expect a reduction of acute and late toxicity on the organs at risk, dominantly the urethra, bladder, penile bulb, and rectum, and an improvement in the quality of life.

studies.name: RTOG 9601
studies.tldr: 12-yr OS 76.3% vs 71.3%, HR 0.77 (0.59-0.99), adding 24mo bicalutamide 150mg to 64.8Gy prostate-bed salvage RT in pN0 post-RP PSA recurrence.
details: 🔍 Double-blind, placebo-controlled randomized trial, enrolled 1998-2003
🔍 760 eligible of 840 randomized; median f/u among survivors 13 yr

subdetails: RP with lymphadenectomy, pN0
pT2 with positive margin, or pT3
Detectable PSA 0.2-4.0 ng/ml ≥8 wk post-RP; median entry PSA 0.6 ng/ml
No prior hormones beyond 2-6 mo preop short-term therapy (6.4%)
CT abdomen/pelvis + bone scan negative for metastases

details: 💊 Bicalutamide 150 mg daily ×24 mo vs placebo, started with RT
🔍 SRT 64.8 Gy/36 fx of 1.8 Gy, 6-10 MV photons, prostate bed + membranous urethra
🔍 No pelvic nodal RT: all pts had negative lymph-node dissections
📊 Absolute OS difference 5.0 points; NNT 20 to avoid one death over 12 yr
📊 No significant between-group difference in non-disease-specific death

details.text: 📊 12-yr OS by PSA at trial entry (post hoc)

details: ⚠️ Subgroups post hoc; interaction significant only for PSA level
📊 Gleason 8-10 OS HR 0.76 (0.44-1.30), p=0.32: few pts, not significant

subdetails: Gynecomastia any grade: 69.7% vs 10.9% (P<0.001)
Late G3 hepatic: 0.8% vs 0.3%
No significant differences in early urinary, bowel, hematologic reactions

details: ⚠️ Bicalutamide 150 mg monotherapy since superseded by GnRH agonists
⚠️ RT QA on random subset only: 64.8% per protocol, 4.4% unacceptable variation
⚠️ Analysis restricted to 760 eligible pts; 79 ineligible + 1 withdrawal removed post-randomization

verdict.rationale: Double-blind RCT, OS primary met at 13y median f/u, but CI upper bound 0.99, agent superseded by GnRH agonists, and benefit concentrated in post hoc higher-PSA subgroups.
verdict.audience: Post-RP pN0 pT2 R1/pT3, PSA 0.2-4.0 ng/ml, salvage RT candidates

studies.significance: The OS gain came with prostate-bed-only RT (64.8 Gy/1.8 Gy, no nodes because all pts were pN0), so it doesn't test hormones alongside an elective pelvic field. Entry PSA splits the read: OS HR 1.13 below 0.7 ng/ml vs 0.45 above 1.5 ng/ml (post hoc), which argues for gating hormone use on pre-SRT PSA.
studies.monday_clinic: In pN0 post-RP pts starting prostate-bed salvage RT at PSA 0.7-4.0 ng/ml, this supports adding long-course antiandrogen therapy; it does not establish an OS benefit at entry PSA <0.7 ng/ml or for node-positive disease.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: **Double-blind, placebo-controlled** randomized trial at NRG Oncology (RTOG) sites, accrual 1998-2003. **840 randomized, 760 eligible** (384 bicalutamide, 376 placebo). Median follow-up among survivors **13 yr**.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Post-RP with lymphadenectomy, **pN0**, **pT2 with positive margin or pT3**, detectable **PSA 0.2-4.0 ng/ml**. Median age 65, median entry PSA 0.6 ng/ml; 74.9% margin-positive, 67.4% pT3.

analysis_sections.label: Regimen
analysis_sections.body: **Bicalutamide 150 mg daily for 24 mo** or placebo, beginning with RT. Adherence ≥18 mo was 69.8% vs 74.7%.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: **64.8 Gy in 36 fractions of 1.8 Gy**, 6-10 MV photons, to the prostatic site, resection bed and membranous urethra, 2D or 3D planning. **No pelvic nodal RT** since all dissections were node-negative.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: **Primary: overall survival.** Secondary: disease-specific death, distant metastases, local progression, non-disease-specific death, second biochemical recurrence, AEs.

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: Late GU G3 **7.0% vs 6.0%**, no excess bowel or hematologic toxicity. **Gynecomastia 69.7% vs 10.9%**; cardiovascular death not significantly higher with bicalutamide.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Alongside GETUG-AFU 16 and SPPORT (RTOG 0534), this forms the randomized basis for hormone therapy with salvage RT, and it is the one of those reporting an **OS** benefit as its primary endpoint. Its agent and nodal-negative, prostate-bed-only field differ from both.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents pN0 pT2 R1/pT3 post-RP pts with PSA 0.2-4.0 ng/ml receiving prostate-bed salvage RT. Does not represent node-positive disease, pts staged with modern imaging, or entry PSA <0.7 ng/ml where no OS benefit was seen.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: RT QA was reviewed only in a random subset, with **4.4% unacceptable variation**. Cardiac events were captured only as reported AEs, so ascertainment bias is possible. The analysis excludes 80 randomized pts deemed ineligible or withdrawn.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The OS gain is modest in absolute terms (**NNT 20 over 12 yr**) but is carried by a halved prostate-cancer death rate with no offsetting rise in other-cause death. The PSA interaction is the actionable signal, and it argues against reflexive hormone use at very low pre-SRT PSA.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: OS benefit came with prostate-bed-only SRT at 64.8 Gy/1.8 Gy, no nodal field, in pN0 pts, so it does not inform hormone use with elective pelvic RT. Entry PSA <0.7 ng/ml showed OS HR 1.13 (post hoc), arguing that early SRT may not need added hormones.
significance_by_specialty.medonc: The agent was 24 mo of bicalutamide 150 mg, now superseded by GnRH agonists, so the OS gain (HR 0.77) informs the principle more than the regimen. Gynecomastia in 69.7% and the PSA-dependent benefit frame whether long-course antiandrogen exposure is worth it at low pre-SRT PSA.

papers.title: Mapping patterns of nodal metastases in seminoma: Rethinking radiotherapy fields
Radiotherapy for Stages IIA/B Testicular Seminoma: Final Report of a Prospective Multicenter Clinical Trial
papers.abstract: Purpose: A prospective multicenter trial was initiated to evaluate the role of modern radiotherapy with reduced treatment portals for stage IIA and IIB testicular seminoma. Patients and Methods: Patients with stages IIA/B disease (Royal Marsden classification) were assessable for the trial. Staging comprised computed tomography of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis as well as analysis of tumor markers alpha-fetoprotein and beta human chorionic gonadotropin. Linac-based radiotherapy was delivered to para-aortic and high ipsilateral iliac lymph nodes. The total doses were 30 Gy for stage IIA and 36 Gy for stage IIB disease. Results: Between April 1991 and March 1994, 94 patients were enrolled for the trial by 30 participating centers throughout Germany. Seven patients were lost to follow-up. Median time to follow-up of 87 assessable patients was 70 months. There were 66 stage IIA and 21 stage IIB patients. One mediastinal and one field-edge relapse were observed in the stage IIA group. In the stage IIB group, there was one mediastinal and one mediastinal/pulmonary relapse. All patients were treated with a salvage regimen of platinum-based chemotherapy. Actuarial relapse-free survival at 6 years was 95.3% (95% confidence interval [CI], 88.9% to 100%) and 88.9% (95% CI, 74.4% to 100%) for stage IIA and IIB groups, respectively. Maximum acute side effects were 8% grade 3 nausea for stage IIA and 10% grade 3 nausea and diarrhea for stage IIB groups. No late toxicity was observed. Conclusion: Radiotherapy for stages IIA/B seminoma with reduced portals yields excellent tumor control at a low rate of acute toxicity and no late toxicity, which supports the role of radiotherapy as the first treatment choice for these patients.

papers.title: Prostate stereotactic body radiotherapy: quantifying intra-fraction motion and calculating margins using the new BIR geometric uncertainties in daily online IGRT recommendations
papers.abstract: Objectives: To measure the magnitude of intra-fraction prostate motion (IFPM) during stereotactic radiotherapy (SBRT) delivered without intra-fraction tracking. To assess if current margins adequately cover IFPM. To derive margins using new guidelines. Methods: IFPM was determined in 20 patients receiving 36.25 Gy in 5 fractions using 97 pairs of pre- and post-treatment cone beam CT (CBCT) scans. Correlation of time between CBCT acquisitions and motion was determined. The magnitude of IFPM was compared to current margins (6 mm isotropic, 3 mm posterior). Margins were calculated using IFPM alone and updated guidelines. Results: The averaged 3D root mean square IFPM was 2.5 mm (4.2 mm). Independent prostate motion was predominantly posterior (70%) and inferior (63%). There was weak correlation between posterior (ρ = 0.38) and inferior (ρ = 0.36) IFPM and time. IFPM greater than current margins occurred in 8 of 97 fractions, six in the posterior direction. Margins were ≤3.5 mm using IFPM alone and ≤3.3 mm Left 3.5 mm Right, 7.0 mm inferior, 3.7 mm superior, 4.4 mm anterior and 3.3 mm posterior using new guidelines, compensating for motion in 92% of fractions. Conclusions: Our current SBRT margins account for 92% of IFPM, predominantly posterior and inferior. Although updated guidelines suggest an increase in margins inferiorly, any increase must be balanced against the possibility of increased toxicity, particularly if biochemical control and side-effects are favourable with current practice. Advances in knowledge: The difference between current clinical margins and those determined using updated guidance is demonstrated. The implications must be considered against clinical outcomes.
